title: The Operating System
description: Explore kernel mode vs user mode, the real cost of syscalls, Linux CFS scheduling, and how cgroups and namespaces became the foundation of containers.

segments.text: The operating system is the most important piece of software you never think about. Every network call, every file write, every memory allocation goes through it. Understanding its internals is critical for diagnosing production performance issues.

Your CPU has protection rings. Ring zero is kernel mode with full hardware access. Ring three is user mode where your application runs. When your code calls read or write, it triggers a syscall that switches from ring three to ring zero. This ring transition costs roughly 100 to 150 nanoseconds on modern x86 hardware.

After Spectre and Meltdown patches, syscall overhead got worse. KPTI forces a full page table switch on every kernel entry, adding another 50 to 100 nanoseconds. This is why high-performance systems like DPDK bypass the kernel entirely for networking, and io_uring was invented to batch syscalls.

Linux uses the Completely Fair Scheduler, or CFS. It models an ideal processor that gives each task an equal share of CPU time. Internally, it uses a red-black tree keyed by virtual runtime. The task with the least virtual runtime runs next. Lookup is O(1) because CFS caches the leftmost node.

Here's a production puzzle I've seen multiple times. Your latency-sensitive service shows periodic 10-millisecond spikes. The cause? A CPU-hungry batch job on the same machine was getting scheduled on the same core, and CFS was giving it its fair share of time.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you prevent a batch job from stealing CPU time from a latency-sensitive service on the same host?

segments.text: The answer is cgroups, or control groups. Cgroups let you limit and isolate CPU, memory, I/O, and network for a group of processes. You can cap a batch job to 200 percent CPU, two cores out of eight, ensuring your latency-sensitive service always has resources. This is exactly what Kubernetes uses under the hood.

Namespaces provide isolation for different system resources. PID namespace gives each container its own process tree. Network namespace gives it its own IP stack. Mount namespace gives it its own filesystem view. There are eight namespace types in Linux, and together they create the illusion of a separate machine.

A container is literally just cgroups plus namespaces plus a layered filesystem like OverlayFS. That's it. No hypervisor, no hardware emulation. When you run docker run, it calls clone with namespace flags, sets up cgroup limits, and mounts the filesystem layers. Container startup is fast because there's no kernel to boot.

But containers share the host kernel. This means a kernel vulnerability affects all containers on that host. In 2019, CVE-2019-5736 allowed container escape through runc. This is why Google runs gVisor, a userspace kernel, for multi-tenant workloads on GKE.
segments.thought_prompt: When would you choose a VM over a container for workload isolation? Think about multi-tenant scenarios.

segments.text: The kernel's memory manager handles page allocation, the OOM killer, and swap. When a process exceeds its memory limit, the OOM killer picks a victim based on oom_score. In Kubernetes, this maps to pod eviction. Setting memory limits too low causes OOM kills; too high causes node-level resource contention.

The I/O scheduler batches and reorders disk requests. For HDDs, the deadline scheduler prevents starvation. For SSDs, the none scheduler passes requests straight through because random access is fast. Choosing the wrong scheduler on NVMe drives adds measurable latency. Always check with cat /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler.

The OS is not a black box. Every syscall has a measurable cost. Every scheduling decision affects tail latency. Cgroups and namespaces are the building blocks of modern infrastructure. When you're debugging a production issue at 3 AM, this knowledge is the difference between guessing and diagnosing.
